tasks.title: Listening 1 — Choose the picture

items.stem: Which project shows how Mariam wants to introduce herself?
items.script: Mariam is preparing a display for visitors who have never met her. She wants them to see her photograph with short notes about what she likes and what she does well. A family tree would show her relatives, and a map would show her neighbourhood. Neither would tell visitors enough about her own interests.

items.stem: Which hobby is Layla most interested in?
items.script: Layla is confident but rather quiet in large groups. Her brother plays football and her cousin enjoys photography. Layla, however, is brilliant at drawing, and she is spending this month learning how to use watercolours. Her family is buying her an art palette for the exhibition.

items.stem: Which picture best shows Rashid's usual behaviour with new classmates?
items.script: Rashid enjoys meeting people. When someone new joins the class, he usually waves, walks over and introduces himself. His brother prefers reading on his own, and his cousin often feels too nervous to enter a room full of strangers. Rashid is the one who makes new pupils feel welcome.

items.stem: Which family tradition is Salma learning?
items.script: Salma comes from a family that enjoys making things by hand. Her uncle plays the oud and her cousin makes pots from clay. Salma is learning from her grandmother to fold strips of palm leaf over and under one another. She hopes to make a small basket for their next family gathering.

items.stem: Which family activity does Rana usually enjoy at weekends?
items.script: Rana says her family sometimes visits the beach and occasionally goes shopping. They usually prefer spending a night outdoors, however, because everyone enjoys talking beneath the stars. They are preparing their tents for this weekend, so camping is the activity she describes in her personal profile.

tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: Why did Huda want to make a personal photo board?
choices: To show that different classmates shared hobbies
To choose a winner for a photo competition
To advertise a new sports centre

items.stem: What did the display include besides photographs?
choices: Hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths

items.stem: How did the pupils collect information?
choices: They offered questionnaires pupils could answer privately
They asked everyone to speak in front of the school
They looked up pupils’ interests on the internet

items.stem: Why were the captions written in Arabic and English?
choices: To practise reading aloud in both languages
To make them easier for more families to understand

items.stem: What did the group do when a pupil changed her mind about a photograph?
choices: They kept her photograph on display
They moved her photograph to another room
They used a drawing in its place

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to our school identity programme. What encouraged you to make a personal photo board, Huda?
Huda: I noticed that classmates who seemed different often shared hobbies, so I wanted to help people discover them.
Interviewer: Did the first display focus only on people's appearance, or did you include their interests as well?
Huda: We included their hobbies, family traditions and personal strengths. Appearance cannot explain the whole story of someone's identity.
Interviewer: Where did your team first collect information for the project, and how did you ask pupils to contribute?
Huda: We visited three classes and offered simple questionnaires. Everyone was free to answer privately or leave a question blank.
Interviewer: When did you begin preparing the photographs, and how long did your work take altogether?
Huda: We started in October and worked for nearly three weeks before the first display was ready.
Interviewer: Who helped you organise the captions, and which languages did you decide to use?
Huda: Our English teacher helped us. We wrote short captions in both Arabic and English so more families could understand.
Interviewer: What happened when one classmate changed her mind about showing a photograph? Did this cause an argument?
Huda: No. We removed her picture immediately and used a drawing instead. Respecting someone's choice matters more than a display.
Interviewer: How did the project change the way students talked to one another at school?
Huda: People began asking about interests rather than making quick assumptions. Several shy pupils also joined clubs that suited them.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage: When Aisha joined a new school in Sohar, she worried that her classmates would not understand her interests. She loved astronomy and usually spent Friday evenings looking at the night sky. Her desk partner, Salma, enjoyed art and was always drawing. At first, the girls had little to talk about. Then their teacher asked the class to organise a display about personal identity. Aisha suggested a simple model of the solar system while Salma offered to design the posters. They invited two other pupils: Hamad, who was confident speaking to visitors, and Noura, who preferred organising details quietly. The project succeeded because each student contributed a different strength. Aisha now believes identity is not only about appearance or nationality; it also includes values, habits, abilities and the way people treat one another. She still enjoys astronomy, but she is learning that sharing an interest can be easier when she listens to other people first.

tasks.title: Listening 1 — Choose the picture

items.stem: How did the students speak to their partner class?
items.script: Our class wanted to ask students in another town about the expressions they use at home. A letter would take several days, and our partner class could not travel to see us. We were able to see their faces on the screen and ask them questions straight away while the call was running.

items.stem: Which device did the team use to keep a record of the interview?
items.script: We wanted to capture our grandparents’ voices and the gestures they made as they spoke. A handheld recorder could only save the sound, and our phone was almost out of power. In the end we put the device on a tripod and used its top microphone to capture both the picture and the sound.

items.stem: How did the visitor communicate with the students?
items.script: The visitor showed us that you can have a conversation without speaking. She did not point to pictures on a board and she did not speak into a microphone. Instead, she made different movements with her hands while using her face to show how she felt. We tried to reply in the same way.

items.stem: What were the pupils recording for their language project?
items.script: Some pupils thought the project would involve reading quietly or typing examples from a book. Our teacher wanted to collect language as people really use it. So I sat with my grandmother and listened as she told me about her childhood in the village. I recorded her voice with her permission.

items.stem: What helped Hana understand the visitor's message?
items.script: At the exhibition, a visitor showed Hana a short message in a language she was still learning. Hana could not find the right page in the leaflet, and she did not need to call anybody. She opened a tool on her phone, chose both languages and showed the visitor the new version of the message.

Text 2. We wanted to capture our grandparents’ voices and the gestures they made as they spoke. A handheld recorder could only save the sound, and our phone was almost out of power. In the end we put the device on a tripod and used its top microphone to capture both the picture and the sound.

Text 3. The visitor showed us that you can have a conversation without speaking. She did not point to pictures on a board and she did not speak into a microphone. Instead, she made different movements with her hands while using her face to show how she felt. We tried to reply in the same way.

Text 4. Some pupils thought the project would involve reading quietly or typing examples from a book. Our teacher wanted to collect language as people really use it. tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: Why did Bilal's class start the project?
choices: Some children understood their grandparents' language but rarely spoke it
The school needed more textbook recordings
Families had asked for a reading competition

items.stem: What type of language did the pupils focus on?
How did the team deal with a problem during the interview?
choices: They wrote out the answers from memory
They checked the batteries and repeated part of the interview

items.stem: Why did two pupils add short English summaries?
choices: So the whole class could learn from the recordings
So the guest could read the questions in advance
So they could shorten the interview itself

items.stem: How did the team protect the families’ privacy?
choices: They removed everyone’s voice from the recordings
They shared only recordings approved by the families

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Today we are discussing how young people can protect languages and share stories. Why did your class begin this project, Bilal?
Bilal: We realised that some children understood their grandparents' words but rarely tried speaking the same language themselves.
Interviewer: Were you studying only written words, or were you interested in conversations and stories as well?
Bilal: We focused on conversations. A language lives through the people who use it and tell stories in it.
Interviewer: Where did your first interview take place, and who was the guest that day?
Bilal: We recorded our first interview at the community centre with my grandmother, who loves telling family stories.
Interviewer: What happened while you were checking the recording, and how did your team respond to the problem?
Bilal: The microphone stopped working for a few minutes. We checked the batteries and repeated that section patiently.
Interviewer: What language did the grandparents speak during the interview? Did you translate anything for younger students?
Bilal: They spoke Arabic, and two pupils added short English summaries so the whole class could learn from them.
Interviewer: When did you share the collection, and how did you protect personal information in the recordings?
Bilal: We shared it on Tuesday during the school exhibition, but we used only recordings that families had approved.
Interviewer: What was the most important lesson you learned about communication through this project?
Bilal: Listening respectfully is as important as speaking clearly. We should ask questions instead of pretending we understand.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage: Last term, Mariam and her classmates were making a short film about communication in their town. They interviewed grandparents who remembered sharing news by letter, and younger people who used messaging apps every day. While they were editing the film, a recorded interview disappeared from the shared folder. Everyone thought the file had been deleted. Mariam was checking the computer when she noticed a message from Bilal. He explained that he had moved the recording to a different folder to protect it from accidental changes. Unfortunately, he had forgotten to tell the team. The students felt relieved, but they also realised that a useful action can cause confusion if nobody explains it. They agreed to keep a simple record whenever a file was moved and to listen carefully when someone raised a concern. The finished film showed more than changes in technology: it showed why clear messages, careful listening and trust matter in every generation.

tasks.title: Listening 1 — Choose the picture

items.stem: Which invention will carry supplies across the valley?
items.script: The village team wants to deliver small parcels after heavy rain closes the road. A driverless car still needs a road, and a wheeled robot cannot cross the flooded path. The engineers are going to try a device with four rotors. It will lift each parcel into the air and carry it across the valley.

items.stem: Which system will Ali use to check whether plants are healthy?
items.script: Ali is developing a useful tool for people who grow vegetables at home. It will not water the plants or switch their lights on. A device will take a close picture of each leaf and send it to a computer. The program will compare the picture with examples of healthy and unhealthy leaves.

items.stem: Which smart-home device will help the family save energy?
items.script: The family is testing a new way to use less electricity at home. They considered a smart speaker and a robot vacuum, but neither manages the heating. Their new device will measure the temperature in the room and turn the heating down automatically when everyone leaves the house.

items.stem: What kind of robot is the team going to build?
items.script: Our team is going to make a robot that collects empty bottles outside. A fixed arm could reach only one spot, and a robot that walks would be difficult to build. We chose a low machine with four wheels that can travel along a path and use a claw to pick up litter.

items.stem: Which device can check the wearer's skin temperature?
items.script: The health club is testing three types of technology. A phone can show a report and an earbud can play a reminder, but neither will touch the skin on the wrist. The device we will test has a strap and a small screen. Its sensor can check the temperature at the wrist.

tasks.title: Listening 2 — Interview

items.stem: What is the science club’s device designed to do?
choices: Check how much exercise people get
Remind older people to drink water
Measure the temperature of a drink

items.stem: How does the device tell someone it is time to drink?
choices: A timer switches on a light and a sound
A phone sends a written reminder
A sensor shakes the water bottle

items.stem: How does the team plan to test the prototype?
choices: At a sports centre with an older student
In the science lab with a teacher and an engineer

items.stem: What problem did the first version have?
choices: The light stayed on all day
It was too difficult to carry

items.stem: What does Noura recommend before designing technology for families?
choices: Ask people about their needs and test ideas carefully
Add more features before talking to anyone
Let the device make all the decisions

tasks.transcript:
Interviewer: Welcome to Future Voices. What kind of technology is your science club developing, Noura, and who might benefit from it?
Noura: We are building a simple device that reminds older people to drink water at regular times during the day.
Interviewer: Did the idea come from a famous inventor, or did someone in your local community suggest it?
Noura: My grandmother suggested it when she forgot to drink enough water during a busy afternoon last year.
Interviewer: How will the device work, and does it use artificial intelligence to make medical decisions for its user?
Noura: A timer activates a small light and a sound. It never gives medical advice; people still make their own decisions.
Interviewer: Where are the students going to test the prototype, and who is supervising the trial?
Noura: We are going to test it in the science laboratory next month with our teacher and a volunteer engineer.
Interviewer: What happened when you tried an early version, and how are you changing the design because of that problem?
Noura: The warning was too quiet, so we are adding a brighter signal as well as a clearer button.
Interviewer: When is your team meeting the engineer again? Is the appointment already confirmed with the school?
Noura: We are meeting her on Wednesday. The school timetable confirms that she will arrive before the second break.
Interviewer: What advice would you give other students who want to design useful technology for families?
Noura: Ask people what they need, test your ideas carefully and remember that technology should support human judgement.

tasks.title: Reading 2 — Short answers
tasks.passage: A group of students at a school in Nizwa is planning a small smart garden. The project will use sensors to measure moisture in the soil, and a simple app will display the results. The students are going to test the first prototype next month. Their science teacher reminds them that a sensor cannot make every decision. For example, the app may report dry soil, but the team must check whether a plant actually needs water before opening the irrigation system. Some pupils think artificial intelligence will make gardening easier; others worry that relying completely on technology could waste water when a sensor breaks. The group is meeting a local engineer on Tuesday to discuss those risks. A school exhibition opens at nine o'clock on Thursday, and the pupils hope to demonstrate the garden there. They will collect feedback and improve the design before producing a larger version. They want to show that useful inventions combine technology with responsible human judgement.
